title: Supreme Court of India’s nod for post facto approval must not be read as support for amnesty schemes
content_html:
India’s environmental impact assessment (EIA) regime rests on a single sequencing rule: a project must be appraised before the pickaxe pierces the ground, not after the building is operational. The Supreme Court of India’s July 29 order, from a Bench led by the Chief Justice of India, Surya Kant, on post facto clearances, reaffirms that rule even as it hollows it out. By quashing the 2021 Office Memorandum while leaving the door open for the Centre to legalise violations through a statutory notification, the Court’s distinction between an administrative order and a notification, is effectively a fig-leaf — a procedural nicety dressed up as respect for environmental norms. The deeper problem that the judgment does not confront is the dissonance between the State-level appraisal machinery and the Centre’s law. When State EIA authorities, expert committees and pollution boards routinely discover violations only after a highway, port or steel plant is built, post facto clearance stops being an exception and becomes the design. Large projects are now appraised as a ‘fait accompli’, their ecological cost weighed only once demolition would cost more than absolution. The Court reasons that governments may frame environmental amnesty schemes much as they do for tax defaults. But the logic that justifies regularising an unauthorised colony for electoral gain cannot be transposed onto works that carve into forests and floodplains. Environmental science exists as a discipline precisely to insist on interconnectedness — that plant, animal, human and microbial systems are bound together, and that damage to one propagates through all. A wetland is not an unregistered plot to be regularised on payment of a fee. Even the argument that these are hospitals and airports meant for public good cannot automatically justify the environmental cost.

Worryingly, that transactional logic now has legal cover. The existing retrospective clearances do exact a fine from those who bypassed the norms — but the Jan Vishwas amendments stripped away the threat of imprisonment for environmental lapses altogether, leaving only monetary penalties thus converting compliance into a ‘cost of doing business’ entry, which a well-capitalised proponent can budget for. The latest judgment does not examine this shift, but endorses its premise, treating environmental harm as a debt that can be settled after the fact. The Court insists that reducing violations to civil penalties does not weaken the precautionary principle. But a principle meant to prevent irreversible harm cannot be honoured by pricing the harm and collecting the cheque. The consequences are incidents of infrastructure projects getting flattened by serious monsoon activity. The Centre would be well advised to read this order not as a licence to multiply amnesty schemes, but as a mandate to repair the clearance apparatus.

title: June’s strong industrial performance is not a sign of things to come
content_html:
The June 2026 data for the Index of Industrial Production has come as a pleasant surprise. The 23-month high growth rate of 7.3% of the overall index was unexpected given the significant economic headwinds from the West Asia crisis and a deficient monsoon. Some of the growth was due to a low base, since the performance last June was the worst in nearly a year, but the numbers nevertheless indicate resilience. The manufacturing sector accelerated due to a dual push from the domestic and the external sectors. Consumer durables growth remained above 7% for the second consecutive month, and the non-durables sector saw growth quicken to a six-month high. At the same time, data from the Commerce Ministry showed that merchandise exports grew 15.5% in June, revealing demand from abroad. The capital goods sector also saw double-digit growth. The sector has grown in double digits in eight out of the last 10 months. This bodes well for the economy, but also reveals some risks. Capital creation, primarily by the government, has been the single consistent engine of growth in the post-pandemic years. It needs to keep firing. There are too many uncertainties and headwinds for other engines such as exports and domestic consumption to consistently take up the load. Other areas of growth are also far too seasonal. The electricity sector grew at a 25-month high in June, largely in response to a heat wave in several parts of the country. The mining sector, too, snapped a four-month streak of contraction and grew in June. Yet, this will likely be temporary since the progressing monsoon will disrupt mining activities.

Economists have also warned that the monsoon’s deficiency will inevitably hit rural demand in the months ahead, which will see the consumer-facing sectors slumping again. Hopes of a ceasefire in West Asia are also evaporating. This is leading to considerable volatility in oil prices, which is sending ripples of uncertainty through the economy. This will play out over the coming months. Planned investments will remain pending, purchases will be deferred, and savings will increasingly overshadow consumption. The economy has displayed resilience so far, but this resilience will be strained as its duration increases. Further, people’s needs are such that simple resilience will not suffice for long. If the external environment is going to remain unfavourable, the government will need to think radically about how to jumpstart the domestic economy. In the meantime, it will have to keep pumping money into capital expenditure even as other fiscal pressures mount.

title: Have fast-track courts delivered on the promise of speedy justice?
author: Aaratrika Bhaumik
content_html:
Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s announcement to set up fast-track courts to hear paper leak cases has once again revived the debate over whether these specialised courts are the silver bullet to India’s chronic judicial delays. Following the announcement, the Delhi High Court has constituted a fast-track court at the Rouse Avenue Courts Complex to exclusively hear cases under the Public Examinations (Prevention of Unfair Means) Act, 2024. However, stakeholders have cautioned that fast-track courts also struggle with mounting pendency and resource constraints. So, have fast-track courts delivered on the promise of speedy justice? Bharat Chugh and Shruthi Naik discuss the question in a conversation moderated by Aaratrika Bhaumik.

How effective have fast-track courts been?

Bharat Chugh: Fast-track courts have succeeded in delivering speed, but only for the limited category of cases assigned to them. That is because, in most instances, a fast-track court does not entail the creation of additional judges or judicial capacity. For example, take the proposed fast-track courts for exam leak cases. The judges presiding over these courts are typically drawn from the existing judicial system and reassigned from the cases they were already handling to hear these priority matters instead. Rather than expand the judiciary’s capacity, fast-track courts redeploy existing judicial resources. As a result, while the designated cases move through the system more quickly, the matters those judges were previously handling are pushed further down the queue.

Shruthi Naik: The larger problem is that we rarely consider, at a structural level, what establishing a fast-track court actually requires. While funds may be allocated for judicial officers, support staff, and operational expenses, the real constraint is judicial capacity. If all we are doing is reallocating existing judges rather than expanding the system, we are simply shifting the backlog elsewhere. Equally important is whether the procedural reforms needed to support these courts are in place. Are witness depositions taking place in a timely and predictable manner? Are all stakeholders coordinating to ensure cases progress without unnecessary adjournments? Without these systemic changes, it is difficult to assess whether fast-track courts are truly delivering on their promise of speedy justice.

The Union Law Ministry recently said that Fast-Track Special Courts (FTSCs) are burdened with a backlog of nearly 2.45 lakh cases. What explains this pendency?

Shruthi Naik: The Law Ministry’s data includes the number of cases instituted, disposed of, and pending over the past three years. A closer look at those figures shows that the case clearance rate (the number of cases disposed of compared with the number of cases instituted) has remained below 100% each year. In other words, the system has consistently failed to keep pace with the volume of new cases being filed. In 2025, around 1.4 lakh cases were instituted, but only about 66,000 were disposed of. The remainder inevitably added to the backlog.

More importantly, if we want to assess whether fast-track courts are truly delivering speedy justice, we need robust data on the time taken to dispose of cases. While the National Judicial Data Grid provides pendency and disposal timelines for courts generally, it does not offer comparable data for FTSCs. Without that degree of transparency, it is difficult to evaluate whether these courts are fulfilling the objective for which they were established.

Bharat Chugh: The pendency in fast-track courts cannot be viewed in isolation. It has to be seen in the context of the overall burden on the justice system. Trial courts across the country are currently grappling with nearly 4.8 crore pending cases, of which roughly 74% are criminal matters. That is an enormous caseload, particularly when viewed alongside the limited judicial strength available to handle it. Every year, crores of fresh cases are instituted, spanning offences from acid attacks and chain-snatching to cybercrime and murder. That is the scale of the challenge confronting the justice system. Without addressing these systemic constraints, it is difficult to expect fast-track courts alone to bring about lasting improvements in the delivery of speedy justice.

The Public Examinations (Prevention of Unfair Means) Amendment Bill, 2026, requires investigations into paper leak cases to be completed within two months and sets a three-month timeline for trials. Should laws prescribe such rigid timelines?

Bharat Chugh: The Supreme Court has repeatedly cautioned against prescribing rigid timelines for criminal proceedings because every case presents its own complexities. Criminal trials often involve chargesheets and evidence running into thousands of pages. Forcing proceedings into a rigid timeline may deprive the defence of a meaningful opportunity to prepare its case, thereby compromising the right to a fair trial. It can also leave courts with less flexibility to effectively manage witnesses, whose testimony is often crucial to the outcome of a case. Therefore, the objective should be to strike a careful balance between expeditious justice and procedural fairness, without sacrificing one in pursuit of the other.

Shruthi Naik: Before prescribing strict timelines, we need to ask whether the necessary institutional capacity actually exists. Do we have enough investigators, forensic laboratories, and judicial resources to complete investigations within the prescribed time? Can forensic reports be generated quickly enough? Can witnesses always be traced and examined without delay? While everyone wants cases to be concluded expeditiously, that objective cannot come at the cost of the quality of justice being delivered. Setting aspirational timelines to encourage the expeditious disposal of cases is one thing, but making them mandatory is quite another.

The Supreme Court has cautioned that arbitrarily designating cases for fast-track courts may violate the right to equality under Article 14 of the Constitution. What considerations should guide the selection of cases for fast-track courts?

Shruthi Naik: Ideally, we should be striving for a justice system that does not require fast-track courts at all. The very demand for specialised courts suggests that people have lost confidence in the ability of the regular justice system to deliver timely justice. More often than not, the decision to assign certain categories of cases to fast-track courts is driven by public sentiment. If individuals are entitled to equal protection of the law, they should also have an equal opportunity to access justice. These are difficult policy choices, and any decision to assign cases to fast-track courts must rest on a rational basis consistent with the guarantee of equality.

In 2019, FTSCs were constituted to ensure the time-bound trial of rape cases and offences under the Protection of Children from Sexual Offences Act. Have these courts lived up to the purpose?

Bharat Chugh: A major challenge facing FTSCs is the acute shortage of resources. Strengthening the prosecution has never received the attention it deserves. Even in Delhi, it is not uncommon for a single public prosecutor to appear before multiple courts in a day, simply because there are not enough prosecutors. This is particularly concerning in complex criminal cases, where prosecutors often face teams of defence lawyers with far greater legal and research support. The same resource deficit is evident in forensic infrastructure. Paper leak cases, for instance, often hinge on digital evidence recovered from electronic devices, making cyber forensics critical. Yet forensic laboratories are severely understaffed and overburdened. Unless we strengthen the prosecution, expand forensic capacity, and fill judicial vacancies, FTSCs alone cannot deliver speedy justice.

What institutional reforms are required?

Bharat Chugh: A fast-track court is only as effective as the investigation that precedes it. If the objective is to deliver timely and well-reasoned judgments, the process must begin with a credible investigation. That requires adequately trained investigators, timely forensic assistance and the support necessary to gather reliable evidence.

Shruthi Naik: Lawyers, witnesses, investigators and prosecutors should know well in advance when they are required to appear so that hearings can proceed without disruption. Equally important is reducing avoidable delays. That means minimising adjournments and ensuring court directions are complied with promptly.

Bharat Chugh is a Delhi-based advocate and former civil judge; Shruthi Naik is a senior resident fellow at the Vidhi Centre for Legal Policy, Delhi

title: Newspaper archives still trump answers generated by AI
author: Suchitra Karthikeyan
content_html:
As I typed in the words, “First Indian leader to visit the Prambanan temple”, in Google search for an article this week, the answer flashed Prime Minister Narendra Modi is the first Indian leader to visit the historic temple. However, I felt a nagging sense of doubt as India and Indonesia have collaborated since the 1940s, both militarily and culturally. To verify, I checked The Hindu’s semantic search which browses through newspaper archives spanning over a century. As reported by The Hindu, on December 14, 1958, India’s President Dr. Rajendra Prasad drove down to Prambanan temple during his official visit to Indonesia. The article titled ‘Monument of Buddha’ noted how Dr. Prasad was impressed by the sight and that he had paid tribute to the renovation work, which was underway with the help of the Archaeological Survey of India.

I asked the same question to various Artificial Intelligence (AI) tools such as ChatGPT, Gemini and Grok, and got the same answer — that Mr. Modi was the first Indian leader to visit the shrine.

To further analyse the extent of AI’s handicap, I questioned both ChatGPT and Gemini about the “first Indian Prime Minister to visit Palestine”; it answered — Narendra Modi on February 10, 2018, when he visited Ramallah in the West Bank and held talks with Palestinian President Mahmoud Abbas. However, a look into The Hindu’s archives shows that Jawaharlal Nehru was the first Indian Prime Minister to visit the Gaza Strip on May 19, 1960. In an article dated May 20, 1960, The Hindu recounts how Mr. Nehru made a one-day trip to the United Nations Emergency Force and Palestinian refugee camps during his official visit to the United Arab Republic (UAR) (a short-lived union of Egypt and Syria). His visit was marred by Israeli Super-Mystere fighter jets circling over the United Nations flight carrying him to Gaza — a violation of the airspace of Palestine which had then been under the UAR’s military control. 

A look into the results given by the AI tools shows that in spite of several newspaper reports of Mr. Nehru’s visit, AI challenged its veracity as Mr. Nehru’s visit was to Gaza — then occupied by the UAR. It chose to classify Mr. Modi’s visit to Ramallah as the first instance as it was governed by the Palestinian Authority. However, India had recognised both Palestine (comprising the Gaza Strip and the West Bank) and Israel in 1948 itself. With the changing nature of the governing authority in both the West Bank and Gaza throughout the years, a visit to either territory by a state head has to be taken into account.

A final example which highlights AI’s limitation came when I posed this query to Gemini and ChatGPT: “Have U.S. senators or Congressmen visited Ram temple in Ayodhya”. Gemini stated that there is no public record or official confirmation of any current or former U.S. Senator or U.S. Congressman having physically visited the temple, while ChatGPT erroneously stated that a U.S. Congressional delegation visited the temple in 2024.

The Hindu’s archival search shows that a nine-member delegation of U.S. Senators visited the Ram Janmabhoomi complex on November 3, 1993, almost a year after the Babri Masjid was demolished. Accompanied by leaders of the Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP), the delegation led by Steven Morse visited the make-shift tent at the site housing Ram Lalla. Mr. Morse clarified that their visit was “to study the democratic functioning and culture of the country” and not for political purposes.

In spite of AI’s continued learning, archives of century-old newspapers like The Hindu present facts without the filter of an algorithm tailored around the user’s preferences, political ideology and search patterns. The above examples show AI’s lack of fact-checking, limited access to older news reports, and failure to remain unbiased. It stresses the need for legacy newspapers to provide more digital reports highlighting its old journalism in order to set the record straight.

A final example which highlights AI’s limitation came when I posed this query to Gemini and ChatGPT: “Have U.S. senators or Congressmen visited Ram temple in Ayodhya”. Gemini stated that
there is no public record or official confirmation of any current or former U.S. Senator or U.S. Congressman having physically visited the temple
, while ChatGPT erroneously stated that a U.S. Congressional delegation visited the temple in 2024.
The Hindu’
s archival search shows that a nine-member delegation of U.S. Senators visited the Ram Janmabhoomi complex on November 3, 1993, almost a year after the Babri Masjid was demolished. Accompanied by leaders of the Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP), the delegation led by Steven Morse visited the make-shift tent at the site housing Ram Lalla. Mr. Morse clarified that their visit was “to study the democratic functioning and culture of the country” and not for political purposes.
In spite of AI’s continued learning, archives of century-old newspapers like
The Hindu
present facts without the filter of an algorithm tailored around the user’s preferences, political ideology and search patterns. The above examples show AI’s lack of fact-checking, limited access to older news reports, and failure to remain unbiased. It stresses the need for legacy newspapers to provide more digital reports highlighting its old journalism in order to set the record straight.

title: The Bay of Bengal as India’s SHANTI anchor
author: Rajeev Ranjan Chaturvedy,Raghvendra Kumar
content_html:
The Bay of Bengal region, one of the world’s most disaster-prone regions, lacks coordinated mechanisms to respond to natural disasters. Non-traditional threats such as climate-induced disasters, illegal fishing, cyber vulnerabilities, and supply chain disruptions require regional cooperation beyond bilateral aid or maritime power. This gap — growing capacity without shared norms — highlights the need for stronger maritime security.

On July 13, External Affairs Minister S. Jaishankar introduced Securing Holistic Advancement through Norms, Trust and Integrity (SHANTI) while launching India’s candidature for the UN Security Council (UNSC) for the 2028-29 term. Building on Security and Growth for All in the Region (SAGAR) and Mutual and Holistic Advancement for Security and Growth Across Regions (MAHASAGAR), SHANTI provides a normative framework for shared maritime spaces, with the Bay of Bengal serving as the ideal region to operationalise it before expanding it across the wider Indo-Pacific.

The Bay’s centrality

In recent years, the Bay of Bengal has moved from the margins to the centre of India’s strategic thinking. Historically, it connected South and Southeast Asia through trade, culture, religion, and the exchange of ideas long before the Indo-Pacific entered diplomatic vocabulary.

Today, it links India’s Act East policy with the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN), provides access to the strategically vital Malacca Strait, and connects the eastern Indian Ocean to major global trade and energy routes. China’s heavy reliance on the strait — often described as the “Malacca dilemma” — has driven its expanding regional presence through ports and infrastructure projects, intensifying geopolitical competition. As economic connectivity, maritime governance, and strategic rivalry converge in the Bay, SHANTI offers a framework that places norms, trust, and integrity — not tonnage — as the currency of durable advantage.

A maritime security evolution

As such, SHANTI can be best understood as a logical evolution of its maritime outreach. SAGAR, articulated in 2015, supplied the vision of ‘equity in development’ and MAHASAGAR, announced in 2025, expanded that vision’s scope recognising the interconnectedness of security (both vertically among nations and horizontally in threat perception) in the wider Indo-Pacific and the Global South. SHANTI offers the grammar of maritime security framework, the norms, trust and integrity in cooperation through which vision can be translated into tangible action that is well received and reciprocated. It shifts the emphasis from competition to demand driven cooperation, from influence to non-prescriptive institution-building, and from episodic crisis management to long-term resilience. This shift — from protecting maritime spaces to governing shared maritime commons — reflects India’s new security mantra. If SAGAR was a statement of intent and MAHASAGAR a statement of reach, SHANTI is a statement of method to situate India as the “preferred security partner” and “first responder”.

Because the Bay of Bengal is a single interconnected system, its cyclones, fish stocks, shipping lanes and pollution cross national boundaries almost by default, and its littoral states face remarkably similar challenges and concerns — disaster risk reduction and response, coastal erosion, fisheries management, port resilience, undersea cable protection and climate adaptation.

Unlike the western Indian Ocean, which is marked by active conflict, fragile economy and contested spaces, the Bay of Bengal’s strategic geography encourages cooperation. Yet, the region suffers less from a lack of institutions than from institutional fragmentation. What is missing is a common framework to align existing mechanisms. SHANTI fills this gap by providing principles to strengthen cooperation in maritime security, disaster response, the blue economy, and environmental resilience. India’s geography gives it a natural convening role, but its centrality should rest on regional stewardship — not dominance — through trust-based, rules-based cooperation among states with shared challenges and opportunities.

Principles to practice

Taken together, these conditions make the Bay of Bengal India’s most governable maritime sub-region — a natural laboratory where SHANTI can move from principle to practice before shaping wider cooperation across the Indian Ocean. This was reflected at the July 2026 Bay of Bengal Initiative for Multi-Sectoral Technical and Economic Cooperation (BIMSTEC) National Security Advisers’ meeting in New Delhi, where member-states adopted common principles for maritime law enforcement and humanitarian assistance and disaster relief. BIMSTEC also agreed to hold its first joint maritime security exercise in the Bay, in November 2026, while a white shipping information-sharing agreement remains under discussion. These initiatives reflect the norm-building and trust-based cooperation that SHANTI seeks to promote. Its lasting contribution, therefore, will not be another acronym in India’s maritime lexicon, but a redefinition of security — from deterrence to resilience, from rivalry to shared responsibility, and from crisis management to governance of the shared maritime commons.

Rajeev Ranjan Chaturvedy is an Associate Professor at the School of International Relations and Peace Studies, and Coordinator of the Centre for Bay of Bengal Studies at Nalanda University, Rajgir, Bihar; Raghvendra Kumar is a Post-Doctoral Fellow at the School of International Relations and Peace Studies, Nalanda University, and a Non-Resident Fellow with the Africa Program at the Foreign Policy Research Institute, Philadelphia. The views expressed are personal

title: Building a universal social safety net for India’s informal workforce
author: Piyush  Kamal
content_html:
Every morning across India’s cities, millions of men and women step out to build infrastructure, deliver goods, and keep domestic life running smoothly. From construction workers scaling scaffolding in metro hubs to gig workers navigating dense traffic, this informal workforce forms the beating heart of the economy. The Labour Ministry’s recent integration of the e-Shram portal with State welfare Boards and job platforms — covering over 300 million registered workers — is a commendable milestone in digital inclusion. For the first time, India possesses a comprehensive registry of its unorganised labour force.

Yet, registration is only the beginning. A digital identity on a mobile screen offers recognition, but it cannot automatically shield a family from a sudden medical emergency, a workplace injury, or the unbearable anxiety of old age.

To understand why policy must move beyond registration, one must look closely at the daily realities of informal work. Over 90% of India’s working population operates in the unorganised sector, where earnings are modest and employment is inherently insecure. Official data reveals that a vast majority of registered informal workers earn less than ₹10,000 a month, leaving virtually no room to build savings or absorb financial shocks. For these households, vulnerability is an everyday reality. A single week of illness, a sudden injury, or a seasonal slump can instantly wipe out months of savings and force families into predatory debt. When human labour is stripped of basic safety, economic growth becomes fragile for the very people who sustain it.

Fundamental flaw

The fundamental flaw in India’s traditional welfare design has been geographic and administrative fragmentation. Historically, social safety schemes have been tied strictly to local residential addresses and fixed occupational categories. When a worker migrates from a rural district in Odisha to a factory in Gujarat, or switches from seasonal farming to urban gig, their access to State welfare schemes frequently breaks down. Inter-State migrant workers, who form the backbone of urban construction and logistics, are particularly penalised by this spatial friction. Local administrative set-ups often demand local documentation that mobile families cannot provide. Consequently, the citizens who need social protection the most are excluded simply because their lives do not fit into rigid geographic boundaries.

Overcoming this barrier requires replacing piecemeal interventions with a unified, portable social safety architecture. India needs a single-window “universal social security account” linked to a worker’s Aadhaar that follows them seamlessly across State lines and job transitions. Financing such a framework does not require fiscal excess; rather, it demands smart, pooled funding mechanisms. A sustainable model can combine central budget allocations with a small, automated welfare cess on digital platforms, logistics operators, and major infrastructure projects. For higher pension tiers, workers could be encouraged to make flexible micro-contributions through digital wallets. By pooling resources across sectors, the state can create a self-sustaining financial cushion for its informal workforce.

What must this portable safety net deliver on the ground? At its core, it must guarantee three essential human protections: immediate accident insurance, seamless healthcare access, and a baseline old-age pension. Health emergencies remain the single largest cause of sudden impoverishment among working-class families. Integrating e-Shram profiles directly with Ayushman Bharat would allow workers to receive cashless medical treatment at any empanelled hospital nationwide, completely free from local ration card constraints. When a health crisis is met with guaranteed medical care rather than out-of-pocket expenses, families do not have to sell their assets or pull children out of school to survive.

Digital public infrastructure such as e-Shram has succeeded in making the invisible visible by giving millions of workers a recognised identity. Now, national policy must fulfill the human promise behind that digital record. True economic development cannot be built on the fragile shoulders of unprotected workers. By converting digital registration into portable, lifelong resilience, India can create a reliable and compassionate mechanism that honours the dignity of labour. It is time to ensure that those who build our cities, harvest our fields, and sustain our daily lives are given the security and peace of mind they so desperately deserve.

Piyush Kamal is a former IRS officer and Honorary Fellow at the Institute for Educational and Developmental Studies

title: Letters to The Editor — July 31, 2026
content_html:
Have constructive debate

As a citizen, it is disheartening to witness repeated disruptions, heated exchanges, and political confrontations in Parliament during debates that could have been devoted to very constructive discussions on issues of national importance. Valuable time has been consumed by arguments, interruptions, and procedural disputes instead of addressing pressing concerns such as the challenges students face, examination irregularities, the quality of education, and unemployment. While differences of opinion are natural in a democracy, they should be expressed with dignity and mutual respect. Both the government and the Opposition share this responsibility. I sincerely hope that our elected representatives will rise above political differences and make Parliament a platform for constructive debate, thoughtful policymaking, and public welfare.

Parry Garg,

Ludhiana, Punjab

The passage of the Bill criminalising acts of disrespect towards Vande Mataram raises an important question: Is this really the most pressing issue before the nation that deserves Parliament’s precious time during the Monsoon session?

India today is grappling with unemployment, examination scandals, inflation, ecological degradation, agrarian distress, border concerns, and institutional challenges. Against this backdrop, debating whether additional criminal provisions are required to protect a song that already commands immense respect among Indians appears misplaced. Laws should respond to genuine and widespread problems, not symbolic anxieties.

One must ask honestly: Who, in any significant number, is insulting Vande Mataram today? If isolated incidents occur, existing legal provisions are already available. Criminal legislation should not become a substitute for political messaging.

The history of Vande Mataram itself deserves to be remembered in its entirety. The decision to adopt only the first two stanzas as the national song was not accidental. It emerged after thoughtful deliberations among leaders such as Jawaharlal Nehru, Rabindranath Tagore and other members of the national movement, who understood India’s extraordinary religious and cultural diversity. They recognised that while Vande Mataram occupied a cherished place in the freedom struggle, national symbols should unite rather than divide.

Their approach reflected prudence, inclusiveness and statesmanship. Ironically, many of the loudest voices claiming exclusive ownership over nationalism today come from political traditions that played little or no meaningful role in India’s freedom movement. Yet they now portray themselves as the sole custodians of patriotism, while questioning the commitment of everyone else. Patriotism, however, cannot be monopolised, legislated or measured through slogans alone.

National honour is not strengthened by creating new criminal offences every few years. It is strengthened when citizens trust their institutions, when Parliament debates people’s real concerns, when constitutional values are upheld, and when governments remain accountable to those they serve.

True respect for Vande Mataram comes not from the fear of punishmentbut from the affection and conviction of the people. Symbols acquire dignity through the conduct of a nation, not merely through harsher statutes.

India deserves a Parliament that spends more time solving real problems than manufacturing symbolic battles. Patriotism is ultimately demonstrated through public service, constitutional fidelity and honest governance—not through political posturing.

Aditya Das,

Bhowali, Uttarakhand

Alleged excesses, remarks

Reports from various sources indicate that brutal force was unleashed against the protesting students in Delhi. Visuals purportedly showing police manhandling young women and using pellet guns, rubber bullets, and spiked lathis, causing bleeding injuries, have gone viral on social media. In this context, some government sources dismissing all this as “normal” only serves to further inflame public sentiment. There have already been objectionable statements describing the young women who participated in the protest in utterly deplorable terms. Any attempt to brush aside these serious allegations is unfortunate.

A.G. Rajmohan,

Anantapur, Andhra Pradesh

title: The next DPI — how India can commoditise AI
author: Srivatsa Krishna
content_html:
India made identity, payments, and data free. Intelligence is next. No other country has deliberately built all three as a digital public infrastructure (DPI) stack at India’s scale. Others have developed only pieces of this. Estonia has a world-class digital identity system, but nothing comparable to UPI. Brazil’s Pix is an excellent free payments rail, but it stands alone. Singapore has Singpass and SGFinDex, while Europe has open banking and data portability. India’s genuine claim to global leadership in public digital infrastructure lies in this unique combination. Its distinctiveness is not any single component, but the integration of Aadhaar, the Unified Payments Interface (UPI), and DEPA/Account Aggregator as interoperable public digital rails.

Between September 2016 and 2019, the cost of a gigabyte in India fell from about $4 to under 30 cents, making it among the cheapest in the world. The result was not a telecom story. It was a civilisational one: 500 million people came online in half a decade, powering India’s digital economy such as payment volumes, the startup ecosystem, the direct-benefit transfers reaching the last village. Aadhaar enrolled 1.4 billion people and turned identity verification from an expensive paper process to a low-cost API call. UPI made digital payments effectively free, processing around 20 billion transactions a month at near-zero cost. India made data free not by subsidising it, but by letting one player absorb the fixed costs of a nationwide 4G network, price at marginal cost, and force every incumbent to match or die.

title: Dalits face hurdles in becoming mainstream leaders
author: Harish S. Wankhede
content_html:
Dalits are important interlocutors in the democratic processes. However, the possibility that Dalit individual leaders will be acknowledged, and accepted, by the general masses as their legitimate representatives has been rare until the recent past. The arrival of Abhijeet Dipke as the popular leader of the Cockroach Janata Party (CJP) challenges this conventional logic of democracy. Dipke’s impressive capacity to lead the Gen-Z movement against the NEET paper leak offers the possibility that a Dalit person can become a popular leader of the mainstream secular movement.

The conventional Dalit Leadership

In nationalist historiography, Dr. B.R. Ambedkar is often labelled the tallest leader who worked dedicatedly to uplift the ex-untouchable castes from the terrible dungeon of caste-based humiliation and precarious menial labour. Though Ambedkar’s association with the agenda of social justice is crucial, overemphasising it often neglects his contribution as a leader of the general masses and as the key architect of the modern nation-state. Such stereotyping and neglect were further used in the post-Ambedkar period to relegate leadership emerging from the Dalit social location. A Dalit person in any party or position is not identified by individual merit or secular credentials but is often judged as a beneficiary of the social justice agenda, nominated to serve the sectarian interests of Dalits.

When Kanshi Ram formed the Bahujan Samaj Party, he proposed an imaginative political collective of the marginalised social groups under the rubric of “Bahujan”. It aspired to unite them, and proposed that they develop their own ideological values and political aspirations against the perpetual domination of the social elites. However, even this aspiration to lead the majority population is devalued and relegated by mainstream political pundits as narrow Dalit politics.

Dalits have formed political parties; however, these outfits remain limited to a small section of the Dalit population and have failed to emerge as an acceptable political force that can serve the social and political interests of others (including the OBCs and Muslims). Because Dalit parties often raise critical challenges against the conventional authorities of the social elites, they are delegitimised as narrow sectarian outfits. Parties such as the Lok Janshakti Party in Bihar or Vanchit Bahujan Aghadi in Maharashtra have received similar allegations that they are incapable of representing the interests of non-Dalits.

‘Dalits cannot lead the others’

The top leadership of national political parties (the Congress, the BJP or the Left parties) has conventionally been dominated by social elites. However, these leaders are not condemned for representing narrow caste interests. Instead, they are appreciated as legitimate representatives of general concerns, including issues raised by marginalised social groups. These parties have occasionally appointed Dalit leaders to key positions of power (for instance, Bangaru Lakshman, Mallikarjun Kharge, and D. Raja) to highlight their keenness to accommodate them and work for social justice. The BJP, for example, has developed an impressive political strategy of “subaltern Hindutva” to engage Dalits and other marginalised social groups, offering them key responsibilities in the organisation and the government. It is expected that Dalits will serve the ideological and organisational goals of the nationalist parties and resist building any independent political assertion.

The Dalit-Bahujan leadership and parties cannot operate with such confidence. Dalits must either operate as a caste-based political outfit or accept token accommodation within the inclusive parties organised by social elites. This binary caricatures the Dalit as merely a caste-body and obstructs the possibility that a Dalit leader or her party can emerge as a legitimate voice of the general masses.

A new beginning

Dipke’s entry into democratic polity brings a radical rupture. Gen Z noticed his Dalit identity but refused to see him only as a Dalit body. Dipke also decided that he is not entering the politics of mass mobilisation only as the voice of the Dalits but as a leader of the aggravated youths. Dipke curated a secular-inclusive image of himself, often downplaying conventional Dalit political rhetoric. His speeches addressed the concerns of affected students, remained critical of the government, and resisted stirring controversy on various sensitive issues.  

For a long time, Ambedkar remained a proud but limited symbol for the protests of marginalised castes. Dipke’s leadership has introduced Ambedkar and “Jai Bhim” as a secular slogan against corrupt political authority and mobilised non-Dalits in this protest. His visible use of Ambedkar’s picture and his promise to abide by constitutional values and the demand for an accountable government have mainstreamed conventional Dalit political concerns. By clubbing the generic students’ issue (paper leak and political corruption) with Ambedkarite ideological values, Dipke has introduced a significant improvisation in mass protest movements.

Future of Dalit leadership

The CJP protest under Dipke witnessed a new form of public protest that has not only allowed Gen Z to occupy centre stage but also instilled a distinct fearlessness and sense of freedom among youngsters to challenge ruling authorities. Furthermore, the camaraderie between the protesting youngsters and Dalit symbols (like the Jai Bhim slogan) offered a new protest culture that heralds Ambedkar and Dalits as the crucial part of contemporary mass movement. This shows that Dalit leadership and Ambedkar’s political ideas are not restricted to the agenda of social justice alone but are capable of providing meaningful leadership to the general public against injustice and corruption.

Harish S. Wankhede is an Assistant Professor at the Centre for Political Studies, School of Social Sciences, Jawaharlal Nehru University, New Delhi
